blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A webhook dispatcher walks a shared `ArrayList` of 12 endpoints on one thread and calls each in turn. An admin thread adds an endpoint about once a day. The team wraps the walk in `catch (ConcurrentModificationException e)` and retries the whole dispatch. What can still go wrong?

options.text: Nothing the retry misses, since the walk throws before it has called any endpoint
options.says: most failed dispatches had already reached some listeners before the walk threw

options.text: Nothing the retry misses, since a walk disturbed by another thread always ends in that exception
options.says: the listener run also ended in NullPointerException and NoSuchElementException, which that catch doesn't see

options.text: Some endpoints get one webhook twice, since the walk throws after it has called the endpoints before it
options.says: most failed dispatches had already reached some listeners, so a retry sends them the event again

options.text: Some endpoints get one webhook twice, since the walk throws only after it has called every endpoint
options.says: the walk fails part-way: giving up never sends the event to the endpoints after the failure, so it had not called them all

origin.section: Once Another Thread Writes, a Fail-Fast Walk Fails at Random; a Small Listener List Needs a Snapshot

questions.stem: Open orders are kept in a `CopyOnWriteArrayList`. During a sale the list grows from 5,000 to 50,000 orders, with about a thousand inserts a second. What happens to the cost of one insert?

options.text: It grows about tenfold, since each insert copies every order already in the list
options.says: every write copies the whole array, so time and allocation per write grow with the list

options.text: It grows about tenfold, since each insert waits for the readers walking the list to finish
options.says: readers take no lock; a walk keeps the array it started with and never holds up a write

options.text: It stays about the same, since an insert only places one reference at the end
options.says: the measured cost per write went from 160 ns at 1,000 elements to 21 µs at 100,000

options.text: It stays about the same, since one copy is shared by all inserts made in the same second
options.says: every mutative operation makes a fresh copy; the bytes allocated per write grew with the list

origin.section: Every Copy-on-Write Write Copies the Whole Array, So Its Cost Grows with the List

questions.stem: An airline moves seats between the cabins of a flight with `cabins.merge(from, -n, Integer::sum)` followed by `cabins.merge(to, n, Integer::sum)` on a `ConcurrentHashMap`. A dashboard adds up `cabins.values()` while upgrades run. What does the dashboard show?

options.text: The seats the flight really has, since each merge is atomic and the walk never throws
options.says: atomic single-key updates don't help: the walk reads each key at a different moment

options.text: The seats the flight really has, since a walk over a concurrent map reads every value at one moment
options.says: no walk over a structure that changes under it gives one moment; the live stock report was wrong in 98 of 100 reports

options.text: Now and then a wrong count, since the walk can read the two cabins of one move at different moments
options.says: a report that reads one side of a move before it and the other after it counts the units twice or not at all

options.text: Now and then a ConcurrentModificationException, since an upgrade can change the map during the walk
options.says: the live reports were wrong and none threw; a weakly consistent iterator never throws ConcurrentModificationException (unit 6.5.3)

origin.section: A Weakly Consistent Walk Fits Work on One Element at a Time, Not a Total Across Elements

questions.stem: Fifty currency rates live in an `AtomicReference<Map<String, BigDecimal>>` that holds a `HashMap`. An update calls `rates.get().put(code, rate)`. A pricing job walks `rates.get()` to convert a basket. Does each conversion use the rates of one moment?

options.text: Yes, since reading the map through the AtomicReference hands the job a copy of its own
options.says: get() returns the one map the updates change; nothing is copied

options.text: Yes, since replacing the value of an existing key cannot disturb a walk in progress
options.says: the job walks the one map that updates change, so a conversion can mix rates from before and after an update

options.text: No, since every update changes the very same map object that the job is walking
options.says: a mutable map kept in the AtomicReference and changed in place is the live map again

options.text: No, since each call to get() makes a new copy and two copies can disagree
options.says: get() copies nothing; the problem is that the one shared map changes in place

origin.section: A Total That Must Add Up Needs a Snapshot or a Lock, and Size Decides Which

questions.stem: An inventory of 2,000,000 items takes about 3,000 moves a second, and an hourly report must add up. The team switches to publishing a new unmodifiable map on every move. What happens to the moves?

options.text: They fall to a small fraction of their rate, since each move copies every entry of the inventory
options.says: the snapshot copies the whole map on every move; at 100,000 warehouses the mover managed a few hundred moves a second

options.text: They fall to a small fraction of their rate, since each move waits while the hourly report walks
options.says: with a snapshot the report walks a map nobody changes, so moves never wait for it; waiting is the lock's cost

options.text: They keep their rate, since only the hourly report ever reads the new maps
options.says: the cost is in writing: each move builds a copy, whoever reads it

options.text: They keep their rate, since the copy is taken once an hour, when the report begins
options.says: the copy is made by every move, not by the report

origin.section: A Total That Must Add Up Needs a Snapshot or a Lock, and Size Decides Which

concepts: Once another thread writes, a walk over a fail-fast collection fails at random, not only with ConcurrentModificationException, and often after it has already handled some elements, so retrying it repeats them.
A snapshot charges each write a copy of the whole map, so it fits small or rarely written data; a lock makes writers wait out each read, which suits large, busy data.
A mutable map kept in an AtomicReference and changed in place is not a snapshot: a reader walks the live map.
A total added up by a weakly consistent walk while writers move value between keys can be one the collection never held, even though each update is atomic.
